#25654. Microbiome home tests are taking off. Can they be trusted?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2514 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Microbiome home tests are taking off. Can they be trusted?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mix of microorganisms from a human faecal sample, imaged using a scanning electron microscope.
  • First, the good news: I have 133 microbial species living in my gut.
  • Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mix of microorganisms from a human faecal sample, imaged using a scanning electron microscope. Credit: Steve Gschmeissner/Science Photo Library.

First, the good news: I have 133 microbial species living in my gut. That’s a collection that ranks as ‘excellent’ according to NirvanaBiome, the manufacturer in Germantown, Maryland, that analysed my stool sample. The firm based its rating on the overall diversity of my gut’s residents plus my levels of specific beneficial and undesirable species.

Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease.

Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease.

But then came a second, less promising assessment: Viome in Bellevue, Washington, identified only 61 kinds of active microorganism in my gut and suggested that some of them were not performing optimally. Viome recommended dietary changes and offered customized supplements to improve my health.

In a recent development, I was intrigued by the results, but also flummoxed by the different messages. That’s not an uncommon response, says microbiologist Rob Knight, director of the Center for Microbiome Innovation at the University of California, San Diego. When scientists tested a handful of microbiome testing kits alongside one another in formal studies, they found wide discrepancies in the results. These differences make it hard to understand or really trust the findings from any given provider, says Diane Hoffmann, director of the Law and Health Care programme at the University of Maryland in Baltimore, who co-authored one of those studies.

According to recent reports, the companies stand by their products. “Of course there’s variability,” states Kelly Moffat, chief operations officer for Cmbio in Germantown, which does the laboratory work and genetic sequencing for NirvanaBiome. “There has to be because this is complex testing.”.

Recent findings suggest that momo Vuyisich, chief science officer at Viome’s lab in Bothwell, Washington, also indicates he was unsurprised by the degree of variation found by formal studies. Labs use different methods to extract, sequence and analyse microbial genetic material. Viome, for example, sequences RNA rather than DNA, allowing it to uncover microbial gene activity, rather than only the presence of genes. Vuyisich argues that this is more relevant to human health. And he says that although every method will have biases, as long as a consumer sticks with the same provider, it should produce results that are comparable over time.

Sources indicate that interest in these kinds of test is booming. “There’s so much public enthusiasm and excitement about the microbiome,” indicates Knight. Some customers are simply curious about the microscopic beings that live inside them and potentially affect their health; others have health conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and hope that their gut microbes will reveal the underlying cause or a path to better health.

Industry observers note that although people can order the tests and follow their recommendations without the help of a medical professional, some people are bringing the findings to their physicians. “I groan when I see someone come in with a microbiome test,” says Fergus Shanahan, a gastroenterologist and immunologist at University College Cork in Ireland, who has spent much of his career studying the microbiome. For someone struggling with gut health, a consumer microbiome profile isn’t usually specific enough to help. And if there’s a concern about an infection, such as Clostridioides difficile, it’s more straightforward to test for known pathogens than to assess the entire microbial community.

The tantalizing links between gut microbes and the brain.

The tantalizing links between gut microbes and the brain.

Microbiologists and gasteroenterologists who spoke to Nature generally agreed that microbiome testing has the potential to both reflect and promote health, but many said that the science isn’t yet mature enough to support microbiome testing for most consumers. In their view, the limited clinical usefulness of today’s consumer tests can make them poor value for money (costing around US$100–300). The specialists warn that acting on advice that doesn’t come from clinicians could lead customers to adopt unnecessarily restrictive diets or delay appropriate medical assessment. Critics say that consumer microbiome testing needs more regulatory scrutiny and oversight.

In a recent development, “This is an industry that’s running wild,” says genomicist Jacques Ravel, director of the Center for Advanced Microbiome Research and Innovation at the University of Maryland School of Medicine in Baltimore and a co-author on one of the studies that tested several providers. With regards to testing methods, he says, “there’s no standard”.

Moffat claims, “I think the jury’s out on exactly what it is that we can actionably do today based on this data.” But she says that microbiome profiles, combined with other testing such as gut metabolomics, could yield interesting and useful health information.

Sources indicate that the gut microbiome has emerged as an incredible correlate of overall health. From immune-system function to metabolism, skin disorders and mental health, study after study has found links between a person’s well-being and the trillions of microbes that live in their digestive tract. The premise of a head count of these species and assessment of their actions, to monitor and improve gut health in a personalized way, certainly sounds appealing. Viome’s website, for example, promises: “No more trial and error … Follow a proposal built precisely for you.”.

Companies can identify species and, on the basis of those lists, infer what the microbes are probably doing, such as manufacturing metabolites or inciting inflammation. But running even the simplest microbiome testing is expensive, indicates Alessandra Cervino, research director at PiLeJe, a science-based food-supplement manufacturer in Paris. She says her microbiome testing company, Luxia Scientific, closed in 2024 for financial reasons.

Some microbiome testing firms recommend fermented foods, such as kombucha, for gut health.Credit: Deb Lindsey for The Washington Post via Getty.

Many testing companies also offer lifestyle and nutritional advice or sell supplements. For example, Viome analysed diverse functions performed by the microbes in my gut, such as digestive efficiency, gas production and serotonin manufacture. I then received a detailed eating strategy — which told me to eschew broccoli and load up on pecans, among other suggestions — along with an offer for precision supplements and probiotics with a price tag of more than $150 a month. Although it’s hard to change the composition of microbes in one’s gut, alterations in diet or even simply ageing can shift their activities, indicates Vuyisich. The firm recommends re-testing every four to six months to check for shifts and revision the plan.

Recent findings suggest that he points to 19 peer-reviewed publications by Viome as evidence of the tech giant’s rigour (see go.nature.com/4actdhq). For example, the firm’s analysis for consumers is supported, in part, by published data on how gut microbes influence individuals’ responses to glucose in various foods, based on 550 people in the United States who collectively ate more than 30,000 meals while wearing glucose monitors1. The company validated those findings in a further cohort in Japan, Vuyisich claims, but those data are not published.

Microbiome tests are not created equal, says Tim Spector, a physician-scientist at King’s College London and co-founder of London-based ZOE, which offers microbiome testing and a supplement in addition to a gut-health app that I’ve been playing with. ZOE’s products, Spector says, are backed by research on thousands of people. “There definitely are some not-so-good players out there that give this field a bad name,” he says. “It’s not easy to do this well.”.

In a recent development, there are also several ways to do microbe testing; companies take varying approaches that yield disparate results, as at least two studies have shown. Scientists at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Gaithersburg, Maryland, shipped homogenized stool samples from one person to seven companies2. NIST’s remit is researching and applying standards for measurement. This experiment was a step towards understanding the diversity of testing options out there, claims one of the study authors, NIST microbiologist Stephanie Servetas, who is based in Sheridan, Wyoming. The researchers didn’t name the companies in their report because they wanted to focus attention on the comparison between tests rather than perceived accuracy of any individual provider.

It has been revealed that the result: “Companies produce strikingly different results,” states co-author Scott Jackson, a molecular geneticist who used to direct the NIST microbiology program and is now a consultant in Saint Michaels, Maryland. “They couldn’t even agree on what’s healthy and unhealthy,” Jackson says. The microbe lists ranged from 34 to 906 identified genera; only 3 of which showed up in all reports. In fact, the results were as varied from firm to company as they would be for different people, despite all tests being done on samples from the same individual.

A European and Canadian team obtained similar outcomes when they sent homogenized samples from one person’s stool to six companies, also anonymized. Three companies rated the microbial diversity as “excellent” or “good”; two called it “average”; one said it was “unfavourable”3. The results were so variable, that at least some of them must be lacking in validation or standardization, indicates co-author Céline Druart, executive director of the Pharmabiotic Research Institute (PRI) in Brussels, a non-profit organization specializing in regulation of microbiome innovations. “It’s very difficult to make a conclusion,” she says.

How gut bacteria could boost cancer treatments.

How gut bacteria could boost cancer treatments.

It has been revealed that this broad divergence in results is not surprising, indicates Jack Gilbert, director of the Microbiome and Metagenomics Center at the University of California, San Diego. The variation starts at sampling: scoop a bit of faecal matter into a tube, stab it with a coring device or swipe the sampler across some used toilet paper; ship it off as-is, or in some kind of preservative (as both Viome’s and NirvanaBiome’s kits asked me to). Each option could influence the balance of the microbes that are collected and what survives to be sequenced.

According to recent reports, in the lab, Servetas states the method by which the researchers extract genetic material from a sample is a major source of divergence. Gentler protocols will bias a sample towards microbes that are easy to crack open, whereas harsher methods will capture a higher share of species with tougher exteriors.

After sequencing, another major source of difference, says Knight, is the bioinformatics pipeline that labs use. What length or number of genetic sequences is required to consider a microbe present? What list of sequences and microbes are they using as a reference? “All bets are off when you then computationally analyse it with your favourite method,” says Knight.

Would companies support having standards to validate their tests? “We are really big advocates on really having a standard here,” says Kimberley Sukhum, chief science officer at Tiny Health in Austin, Texas, which offers gut microbiome tests as well as vaginal microbiome tests.

In a recent development, but it’s hard to set those standards, in part because there is no known ‘ground truth’ for a natural microbial sample. Compare that with, say, a blood-glucose test; a lab can get a known value from a standard sample either right or wrong. But the microbiome, in its glorious complexity, does not allow for such simple validation. NIST has used mixed human donor samples to develop a standard4. And Tiny Health has experimented with generating a reference for benchmarking from synthetic communities. It was built from individual microbial species rather than sampled from faeces5. But neither of those standards is exactly like the microbiome of an individual person.

According to recent reports, even if labs could assess a microbiome perfectly, they’d still have a problem: there’s no defined healthy microbiome like there is one range of healthy blood-glucose levels. Each person’s microbiome is unique, like a fingerprint. There are infinitely many ways to have a healthy microbiome, and infinitely many ways to have an unhealthy one, notes Shanahan; it’s not entirely clear how to draw a line between the two.

How gut microbes could drive brain disorders.

How gut microbes could drive brain disorders.

Recent findings suggest that companies must compare customer microbiomes with some standard of health, but these vary too. They might be based on past customers or large, public databases. But microbiomes differ considerably depending on factors such as ethnicity, sex, age, recent antibiotic use or even whether someone was born by caesarean section.

#25653. Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

📅 23 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1041 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1041 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.
  • Industry observers note that "People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW.
  • The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

Industry observers note that "People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it.".

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

Industry observers note that "A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity.".

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

According to recent reports, but a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer mentioned their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages.".

According to recent reports, research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on.".

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'".

It has been revealed that later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she noted.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to.".

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions.".

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'".

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point.".

Sources indicate that but the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there.".

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum mentioned.

Tiny describes a similar ambivalence.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it.".

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

In a recent development, online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered.".

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny.".

By NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Mauricio Pochettino has vowed to reset the culture at Manchester United as he lifted the lid on being in the stands in 1999 to see the club's greatest triumph.

Pochettino was officially appointed as United's newly introduced head coach on Wednesday and took charge of training for the first time on Thursday.

The Argentine was pictured greeting his new squad, with several stars having returned from international duty, before attentions turned to preparing the Red Devils for Sunday's trip to Anfield.

Pochettino also addressed the club's internal media team for the first time, outlining how he looks to drag this underperforming squad up the table.

'The culture is the most important,' Pochettino explained.

'Create the habits, the principles, and I think that is what we want to create.

Mauricio Pochettino took Man United first team training for the first time on Thursday.

Matheus Cunha and Lisandro Martinez were among those to report back after international duty.

Man United will hope to hit the ground running under Pochettino when they face Liverpool on Sunday.

'We need to [be] looking forward and to find a way to create the best habits and the culture that makes us to be close to winning every single game.'.

According to recent reports, 'The players need to express their talent. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now – it's to work with them and try to take the pressure.'.

Pochettino's determination to be the man to bring winning football back to Old Trafford is in large part due to one of his founding memories of the club back in 1999 when he was a player at Espanyol.

Alongside his now trusted goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez, Pochettino was at the Nou Camp to see United clinch the Champions League, thus sealing a famous Treble, against Bayern Munich.

Sources indicate that 'In 1999, I was in Barcelona for that final. That was an iconic final,' he added.

Industry observers note that 'Toni Jimenez [was there] too. We were shouting for Manchester United from there. I was so excited to see Manchester United.

In a recent development, 'This [is the] type of game that you stay sitting in your place [for] and you're so excited because you are watching the game. That was an amazing game.

It has been revealed that 'And then what happened in the end... it's like it's impossible not to empathise with that team, no?

'That was an amazing memory that made me pay more attention to United, to [Sir Alex] Ferguson and the players that were there, that are all legends.'.

That level of success feels a lifetime away from the current squad, which emerges from the international break for a trip to face bitter rivals Liverpool at Anfield slumped 18th in the Premier League.

Pochettino wants to focus on the potential of his Man United squad, rather than their current Premier League plight.

Pochettino is determined to shift the culture at Manchester United back to winning.

The Argentine head coach was in the stands in Barcelona cheering for United back in 1999.

While there are those who may be daunted trying to turn around the ship which sunk so far it cost Michael Carrick his job, Pochettino wants to focus on potential, rather than the present.

'It's a mistake to see the [current] situation. We need to see the potential of this club,' a defiant Pochettino added.

Sources indicate that 'Of course, the circumstances are the circumstances, and we need to be responsible for the circumstances. But at the same time, we need to understand that it's a game and, to connect with the game, we need to feel free.

'The players need to express their talent. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now – it's to work with them and try to take the pressure [off].

It has been revealed that 'Pressure needs to bring energy, responsibility needs to bring energy. Because if not, it's too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back.

'When you connect with the game, you connect through your talent and when you feel freedom, when you feel happy, when you want to play for your team-mates, when you want to play for your family, when you want to play for your club, your fans.

'That is what we need to create all together and I think we have an amazing staff - we were talking a lot today. Then [we need to] settle all the principles and the ideas and to create our own philosophy and start from zero.

'I think with the power of this club and the fans supporting us, I think we will get in the place that we deserve to be.'.

Pochettino touched down in Manchester on Wednesday morning after his overnight flight.

Pochettino poses at his unveiling with United director of football Jason Wilcox on Wednesday.

Pochettino knows that time is not on his side ahead of an upcoming week that sees United travel to face Liverpool on Sunday, followed by a Champions League trip to face Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday. The week is rounded out by a home match a week on Saturday against Brentford.

The Argentine head coach touched down in Manchester on Wednesday morning, taking a private jet straight after the final whistle of United States versus Haiti in Cincinnati.

In a recent development, from there he immediately headed to their Carrington training base where he took a tour and met players and staff, including Tom Heaton, Luke Shaw, Mason Mount and Bruno Fernandes. It is understood he left a good first impression on the players.

And yet, in spite of such a packed schedule, which saw him leave Carrington very late at night on Wednesday and reappear bright and early on Thursday for training, Pochettino is raring to go and is eager for his players to head to Anfield on Sunday convinced they can win.

According to recent reports, 'I have plenty of energy. It's a privilege to be head coach of Manchester United,' he mentioned.

Sources indicate that 'And we are not wasting time. We need to be ready to compete on Sunday.

Sources indicate that 'Now it's not time to think about rest, it's not time to think about sleep. It's about being ready and to prepare everything to be sure that we are going to compete in the best condition at Anfield.'.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion at 20 years and 68 days old on Sunday when he finished third in the Mexico City Grand Prix behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.

The previous recordholder was Germany's Sebastian Vettel, who first became a world champion at age 23 in 2010.

Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953.

Sources indicate that "I'm speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened," remarked Antonelli after finishing the race.

His parents and sister were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car.

He was then mobbed by his pit crew.

"It's been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max ​and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future," the 20-year-old said.

Antonelli, who secured the title with four races remaining, said the final lap was complicated by the excitement of what he had achieved.

"I think I lost two seconds because I could not see ahead, I think I saw two Ferraris," he stated. "It was very special, a lot of memories went through my mind at that moment, and I let it all out after achieving one of my biggest dreams.".

Antonelli has now risen to 380 points with four races remaining. Verstappen (261) snuck past Hamilton (259) in the standings, but they will be racing for second the rest of the ​way.

Antonelli started the race in ​fourth and needed to finish ‌ninth or better to secure the championship on Sunday no matter what his peers did.

He had a relatively smooth run, though the race was interrupted by a red flag around Lap ​45 when Valtteri Bottas crashed.

Verstappen, meanwhile, claimed his sixth victory at the Mexico City Grand Prix, further cementing his affinity with the circuit.

After Mexico, F1 will head to Brazil and then to Las Vegas.

The final two Grands Prix are scheduled to be held in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. But it remains uncertain whether they will take place, given the geopolitical instability in the region.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CRAIG HOPE, CHIEF FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 12:49 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 05:54 EST, 20 November 2026.

This time, Matthias Jaissle wants his fingerprints on the bank notes. But what the head coach wishes for in January, and what Newcastle United are willing and able to give, is likely to be very different. When that happens, it rarely ends well - on the pitch or off it.

The need for reinforcement is clear, even on the back of £270million invested in the summer. Jaissle knows as much and is not afraid to say so. The rookie German has to protect himself as much as he does his club.

According to recent reports, because, as Newcastle prepare for what threatens to be a long and testing winter, Jaissle is revisiting the brochure presented to him in the summer. And that is the 38-year-old's concern and frustration - the prospectus for the season ahead was not of his making.

He arrived three weeks before the start of the campaign and with four of eight signings already through the door. At a cost of £110m, that quartet have started just three Premier League games between them, and each of those by teenager Sean Steur. Baz Toure and Aladji Bamba are virtual spectators, while reserve keeper Ewen Jaouen is injured.

For Jaissle, you suspect, that money was not spent as he would have advised, had he been in situ. Now, in the fresh year, he wants greater control, as well as a No 10 and No 9. For any Newcastle follower averse to tension, you best watch this transfer window through your fingertips.

Jaissle, sporting director Ross Wilson and chief executive David Hopkinson are the protagonists who will navigate January. At least, that is, if Jaissle makes it into 2027. He deserves that time - not least because of the turbulent and transitional situation he inherited - but the next four fixtures will potentially make or break him and the season.

Head coach Matthias Jaissle is seeking greater control of Newcastle United's transfer strategy.

Aladji Bamba has been a virtual spectator and joined in the summer before Jaissle's arrival.

After the visit of league leaders Arsenal on Saturday, there is a trip to second-placed Brighton, followed by a seismic home double header in the space of five days against Mauricio Pochettino's Manchester United and bitter rivals Sunderland.

It is why, despite rumblings behind the scenes in recent days of potential transfer discord, Jaissle was on message - the collective, club message - when I asked him about the profile of player he might want in January.

'It's not the time to talk about the transfer window,' he said. 'We have players capable to deliver higher performances on the pitch. We have major quality, not only up front, but throughout the whole squad. We believe we can do better and this is what we now want to influence.'.

Industry observers note that however, there was a softening when I sympathised with the head coach over him being judged by a window for which he did not have ownership. Did he, then, want more influence this time?

'Now, it's a different story (compared to the summer), if you're already in and also if you have clarified your clear idea, your clear needs, it's going to be easier,' he said.

Recent findings suggest that 'But the transfer market is still a long time ahead, at least it feels like that right now with our fixtures. Our task, especially from my stance, is to focus on the next match and the upcoming challenges.'.

Jaissle knows that his case will only be strengthened by a steadying of results, even though, conversely, more defeats would heighten the need for signings. They have lost four from six in all competitions.

According to recent reports, the problem is that the hierarchy are on the record as stating the summer business went pretty much exactly as they wished and believed they had a squad for the entire season. There are also Squad Cost Ratio limitations. It is understood there is headroom for one player, but not the two the manager would prefer and not at a fee approaching the £51m they paid for Matias Fernandez-Pardo on deadline day.

Jaissle wants a upcoming No 9 to compete with the likes of Yoane Wisse who has one league goal.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo (left) has failed to impress so far at Newcastle after his £51m arrival.

According to recent reports, the 21-year-old forward is another problem. He is still to score from seven appearances and there is a fear he is not yet strong enough for the Premier League. Interestingly, Jaissle revealed on Thursday his dismay that he was booked during the 1-1 draw at Fulham last time out for screaming at Fernandez-Pardo to stand up.

That is not to say Jaissle does not believe in the talent of those brought in. He does. But for a coach in his first season in a major European league, he needs players who can impact today, not tomorrow. He needs, and wants, more experience. One of his first recommendations in August was to sign 31-year-old midfielder Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg. Nico Gonzalez eventually arrived in that position, but the 24-year-old looks like a player who has spent two seasons in reserve at Manchester City.

So, it is easy to see why Jaissle needs and wants more in January. It is also easy to see why he might not get it. There could be trouble ahead, and that is not just the upcoming matches.

Estêvão has made just two starts under Alonso, both in this competition. “The season is long and there will be moments for everyone,” Alonso said.

It was hardly a ringing endorsement especially as Alonso brought on Emegha instead. It is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Industry observers note that liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

“There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola remarked ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”.

Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitike remain long-term absentees for the hosts with Jeremie Frimpong also missing. Florian Wirtz could feature despite going off with an ankle knock during the win over Brighton.

It has been revealed that like Liverpool, Chelsea also had an all-Premier League tie in the third round of this competition, beating Leeds 6-3 in a high-scoring affair at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea come into tonight’s game off the back of a 2-0 defeat against Tottenham in the league last weekend. Not only did they lose on Saturday but to make matters worse for them Cole Palmer was sent off. As a result of that red card, Palmer is suspended for tonight’s tie.

Recent findings suggest that “We [Alonso and Palmer] spoke and for sure he knows the mistake he made,” Alonso noted. “Things that you can avoid. I hope that this is not going to be repeated. He is aware of that, he is mature and it was a mistake. He is in a good space, he connects very well socially with his teammates. They like him, they want Cole smiling, they want Cole having fun, enjoying his game because when we see that, he will have a better team. I will just ask you because he has got this very cool persona, you probably know his personality is very interesting.”.

Former Liverpool midfielder and current Chelsea boss Alonso has lost his two games as a manager against Liverpool; a 4-0 defeat as Bayer Leverkusen boss and then a 1-0 loss when in charge of Real Madrid, with both taking place at Anfield. Alonso is not the only ex-Liverpool midfielder to return to Anfield tonight as their former captain Jordan Henderson is in the Chelsea squad for tonight. Joao Pedro has missed the trip to Anfield because of a thigh injury which could rule him out for a few weeks.

The Premier league fixture between these sides at Anfield ended in a 1-1 draw back in May. In that match, Arne Slot was in charge of Liverpool with Calum McFarlane in interim charge of Chelsea. Chelsea won the reverse fixture 2-1 at Stamford Bridge. Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.

Three of Everton's Premier League fixtures in January – including the Merseyside derby at Anfield – have been moved for live television coverage.

The Toffees' trip to Coventry City remains on Saturday 16 January, but with an earlier kick-off time of 12.30pm (GMT), and will be shown live on TNT Sports.

The following weekend, David Moyes' side will now host Brentford at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Sunday 24 January, in a 2pm (GMT) kick-off that will be broadcast live on Sky Sports.

Finally, the Merseyside derby against Liverpool at Anfield on Saturday 30 January will now take place at the earlier time of 12.30pm (GMT) and will be live on TNT Sports.

Keep an eye on evertonfc.com and the Club's social media channels for ticketing updates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .

"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," noted local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

Recent findings suggest that the ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.

Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

Recent findings suggest that "In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site.".

Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property.".

LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.

Recent findings suggest that california's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

According to recent reports, today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.

It has been revealed that under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," noted Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.

Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.

LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.

California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman remarked energy companies were prepared to challenge the new ordinance.

Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.

"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," remarked Zierman.

The relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

It has been revealed that even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

According to recent reports, california's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.

In a recent development, when wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.

But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging looks or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.

But those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.

A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup."  For now, she is states both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air.".

Breaking: How to make AI data centres more sustainable

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AI companies must engage with those who oppose the expansion of data centres.Credit: Michael M.
  • Recent findings suggest that around the world, people are demanding a halt to the proliferation of data centres — racks of computers, housed in warehouses, that are powering the boom in artificial intelligence.
  • People have many concerns about the way AI is being developed, including how it might affect safety, security and jobs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that AI companies must engage with those who oppose the expansion of data centres.Credit: Michael M. Santiago/Getty.

Recent findings suggest that around the world, people are demanding a halt to the proliferation of data centres — racks of computers, housed in warehouses, that are powering the boom in artificial intelligence. Communities worry that existing infrastructure will not be able to handle the surge in demand for electricity and water, and that data centres’ energy demands will cause environmental and health problems, including increases in air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions. The question of whether AI is going to stall climate action is explored in the first of a three-part Nature Podcast (Nature https://doi.org/rzqs; 2026).

Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say.

Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say.

People have many concerns about the way AI is being developed, including how it might affect safety, security and jobs. Where energy is concerned, however, any added demand for computing power can, and must, be met in smart, sustainable ways, not by burning more fossil fuels. Achieving this will take some creative thinking, and researchers need to be closely involved. Many argue that there are alternatives to relying on energy-intensive data centres, such as AI models that can run on individual computers or institutional servers, thereby consuming much less power than those run using cloud services. Efforts to develop such options need to be better funded.

Future projections of data centres’ energy demands are hard to make, because they are based on assumptions that could change. If current global trends continue, electricity consumption by data centres will go on rising. Between 2017 and 2024, it grew by around 12% per year. Figures for 2024 from the International Energy Agency (IEA), based in Paris, show most of this demand coming from three regions: the United States (45%), China (25%) and Europe (15%).

The Electric Power Research Institute, a non-profit organization in Palo Alto, California, has projected that the continued growth of US data centres could add up to 94 gigawatts of demand by 2030, equivalent to 17% of the country’s electricity consumption. Data centres currently consume more than 1.5% of the world’s electricity supply, and the IEA’s projections indicate that this figure will more than double in the next few years. By 2030, data centres could consume more electricity than Japan, the agency states.

Why scientists should lead the shift away from AI mega data centres.

Why scientists should lead the shift away from AI mega data centres.

It has been revealed that there are serious concerns that this extra demand will be powered mainly by fossil fuels, when carbon emissions are already at a record high. Research published this week in Nature Sustainability estimates that some 400 data centres in the United States accounted for around 26 megatonnes of carbon dioxide emissions between May 2024 and April 2025, more than those produced by many countries (G. Guidi et al. Nature Sustain. https://doi.org/hcsptc; 2026). And according to a study published last week in Nature Climate Change, data centres’ energy demands could prolong the lifespan of coal-fired power stations (C. Li et al. Nature Clim. Change https://doi.org/rzqr; 2026).

Recent findings suggest that but none of this is inevitable. Governments could mandate that upcoming energy demand be met with renewable sources. And regulators could look at alternative ways to manage existing electric supplies.

Industry observers note that many nations’ electric grid systems are designed to accommodate surges in demand, whether to power extra cooling on hot summer days or extra heating during winter cold snaps. Much of the time, there is excess capacity. This excess could be used to reduce the amount of new energy needed to power data centres.

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown.

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown.

According to recent reports, one solution is to curtail data-centre operations during periods of peak electricity consumption, and ramp up at times of lower demand. An analysis released in 2025 by researchers at Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, found that the US electric grid could accommodate 98 gigawatts of extra demand in this way, without adding any new generation capacity (see go.nature.com/4cdeknm). That 98 gigawatts would be enough to cover most, if not all, of the expected expansion in US data centres over the next few years.

Sources indicate that there is potential for this to become a reality. In June, as part of a larger effort to modernize the grid, the US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission instructed grid operators to draw up a plan for how they will cope with extra demand from data centres. The technology industry is understandably paying close attention to how it might mitigate the problems of powering data centres. Earlier this month, OpenAI announced what it is calling a “grid protectors program”, a project to consult with US grid operators, regulators and policymakers to see how the company can work around peaks in power demand.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Google is paying households and businesses in parts of the Eastern United States to reduce their electricity consumption during periods of high demand. Similar proposals are being considered in other countries.

Why open-source generative AI models are an ethical way forward for science.

Why open-source generative AI models are an ethical way forward for science.

In a recent development, these are all tentative moves in the right direction, although arguably progress is not being made fast enough. Policymakers and data-centre operators must engage seriously with those who oppose the centres’ expansion. At a minimum, any new energy sources developed to power these centres must be renewable. Existing energy sources can also be better deployed, and researchers working to develop alternatives to energy-intensive data centres should be better supported. More peer-reviewed evidence is needed, especially for countries outside the United States.

It has been revealed that there are smarter and more sustainable ways to power the growth of AI, but to achieve them, concerted and coordinated action will be needed. In this way, the harm posed to people and the planet can be minimized, and AI technologies can benefit everyone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the substantial screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

According to recent reports, had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

In a recent development, jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

In a recent development, the lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the complications Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

It has been revealed that thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

In a recent development, thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N.

Recent findings suggest that the last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major concern for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a big day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

In a recent development, “We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”.

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

It might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

In a recent development, what they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

Sources indicate that james Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU.

The roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

Recent findings suggest that hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

Hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI.

It must be said the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

Sources indicate that the whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

He did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Lausanne-based court had ruled that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to take part in ice hockey world championships again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The president of the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), Franz Reindl, unveiled shortly after the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday, that he had called a meeting of its main decision-making body for Monday and Tuesday.

The Lausanne-based court had ruled that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to take part in ice hockey world championships again. They had been barred from doing so since shortly after Russia released its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"Our task now is to implement this ruling responsibly," remarked Germany's Reindl, who was elected IIHF president just last month.

In a recent development, "Several championships are only weeks away, and changes to participation affect many people; players, teams, organizing committees and host cities," he noted. "We will work closely with all of them to find practical solutions.".

The first tournament the CAS decision applies to is the World Juniors, to be held beginning on December 26 in Canada. Just how it will affect the tournament is not clear. Hockey Canada stated it was in contact with the IIHF and had briefed Prime Minister Mark Carney's government on the decision.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand told public broadcaster CBC that she is "not comfortable" with allowing a Russian team to take part in the tournament in Alberta.

It has been revealed that "This is a very unwelcome decision given the geopolitical situation, given the actions of Russia," she stated. "All options are on the table, and I will say, again, I greet this decision with great disappointment.".

Canada's secretary of state for sport, Adam van Koeverden, appeared to rule out Russian athletes being granted visas for the tournament.

"Canada will maintain restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes at events hosted in Canada that receive funding from the Government of Canada and explore further options to ensure that the Russian government is held accountable," he stated in a statement.

Germany is also considering its options as it prepares to host the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Düsseldorf and Mannheim in May.

"The German government takes a very critical view of the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, a government spokesman remarked on Sunday, according to the DPA news agency.

"The German government will discuss possible consequences of the ruling, including for the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany, with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) promptly.".

It has been revealed that the DEB's chief executive, Frank Lutz, is to travel to Berlin to discuss the matter with government officials this week. Speaking on broadcaster MagentaSport on the weekend, he conceded that surrendering Germany's hosting rights for the lucrative tournament was a possibility.

"I do not want to paint a black picture. I do not want to call the World Championship into question either. But of course, we at the DEB also have to consider the option of handing back this championship," he said.

Several other national ice hockey federations have expressed disappointment at the CAS decision, including those of Ukraine, Sweden, Finland, and Czechia.

Sources indicate that the International Olympic Committee opened the door for Russian athletes to return to international competition when it lifted its ban of the Russian Olympic Committee in July. However, the IIHF had already decided to continue to exclude Russian teams for the 2026-27 season – over security concerns. The CAS decision – handed down after an appeal by Russia – found this reasoning was insufficiently proven.

The Kremlin's reaction to the ruling was, unsurprisingly, positive.

Recent findings suggest that "Russia is returning to world hockey. This place rightfully belongs to us, and discrimination in hockey has been brought to an end," Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev told state television channel Vesti.

A boycott of the World Juniors, Men's World Championships or other tournaments by individual nations is now emerging as a real possibility.

"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen stated in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday evening.

"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.

By Tuesday afternoon, the Finland-led effort was gaining steam, with Sweden, Norway and Denmark making similar statements.

"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson stated in a statement.

This came shortly after Norway said it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.

Sources indicate that "Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors tournament.

There has been the suggestion, that having won this victory at the CAS, Russia's next focus could be on football, where its national and club teams remain excluded from international competitions.

Russian FA general secretary Maxim Mitrofanov told state news agency Tass that there "should be one rule for all.".

World football's governing body FIFA allowed a Russia boys' team to play under its national flag in the inaugural Under-15 World Cup and Festival in Azerbaijan, which kicked off last week and ends on Saturday.

This article was originally published on November 2, 2026. It was updated on November 3 with the statement from the Finnish Ice Hockey Association. It was later updated with the statements from the Swedish, Norwegian and Danish federations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 09:55 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 09:55 EST, 20 November 2026.

St Mirren manager Craig McLeish claims self-interest and poor governance are killing Scottish football’s hopes of improvement.

McLeish is frustrated that Scottish Football Association chief football officer Craig Mulholland has reportedly had to dilute looks for young player quotas to appease five William Hill Premiership clubs.

Mulholland was hoping to ensure teams featured Scotland Under-21 eligible players for an average of 60 minutes per league game and had two on the pitch for each cup tie.

McLeish mentioned: 'That’s damning that he’s having to change his plans to pander to clubs who aren’t really on board with it and don’t really have the best interests of the Scottish national team at heart.

Industry observers note that 'I understand why. We have owners from outwith this country. We have managers from outwith this country. They’re in jobs, they’re all fighting for their clubs.

'But why then are those people allowed to be the ones that hold the keys to the future of our country and the development of our national team?

St Mirren boss Craig McLeish believes self-interest at clubs is hampering Scottish football.

'It’s the way governance is set up and we’ve killed ourselves with that because the people who actually have a say in it have, not have no interest but they’ve got self-interest, and there’s a lot of self-interest at the top end.

Industry observers note that 'I just don’t see a way that we can really properly change unless something to do with governance changes and I just don’t ever see that happening. It’s really sad.'.

Although McLeish backs quotas, he fears that would not address the root cause of Scottish football’s problems.

'We always focus at the top end, what our league size is, quotas for young players, a national base,' remarked the 36-year-old, who worked in St Mirren’s youth academy before his current role.

'We have a fundamental problem that starts at our youngest age groups, at four and five years of age, about how we actually teach kids to play. And until you fix that, you can’t fix the top end of it.

'It’s crazy some of the stuff that’s going on, the formats, how we teach kids. There’s just a massive lack of education and expertise at the very bottom of our pathway.

'In this country, football’s everyone’s sport and everyone gets access to it but if you take your young kids along to swimming or gymnastics or whatever other sport, you’re there with properly qualified coaches, teachers who have maybe done things at the top levels of that sport.

'We have nothing without the volunteers that work at the bottom end of the grassroots game, but they’re not teaching kids how to play football properly, in my mind.

'And you’re just hoping that they get put with a volunteer coach that can teach them something, that they get in with a really good group at the youngest ages.

Sources indicate that 'Because that development between the ages of three and eight, if you don’t get that right, you’re dead. You can’t do anything after that point, and we don’t do it well enough. And you’re just chasing yourself and we’ll never catch up.'.

The SFA has been contacted for comment.

Could the AI boom make borrowing more expensive in Europe?

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.
  • Industry observers note that four of the Significant Five hyperscalers — Amazon, Google owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued about $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools.
  • Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Substantial Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.

Industry observers note that four of the Significant Five hyperscalers — Amazon, Google owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued about $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros.

Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Substantial Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.

Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING.

That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like France, Germany and Italy, whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances.

According to recent reports, with public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%.

The French government's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion right now to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.

Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance.".

Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market.".

That means governments and international lenders such as the European Union and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow.

Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance.".

Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest.

Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and company borrowing costs rose together.

Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022.

The bank's analysts noted this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period.

Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments.

Industry observers note that the pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom.

A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development(OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise.

Sources indicate that "Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.

While AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, US Massive Tech's huge appetite for capital could add further pressure next year, due to the additional billions in upcoming bonds planned.

The irony is that European taxpayers could end up paying more on their own governments' debt, partly to help finance an AI boom across the Atlantic.
